ch41.b.d.N: Number $N$ of identical wells (atoms) in a row
ch41.b.d.b: Width $b$ of the barrier between neighbouring wells; smaller means closer atoms
ch41.b.goal.split: When $N$ identical wells come close, each level splits into $N$ levels
ch41.b.goal.gap: For large $N$ the split levels fill continuous bands, separated by energies no electron can have (the band gap $E_\text{g}$)
ch41.b.obs.two: Two wells: each level splits into a pair (the double well of Ch 39)
ch41.b.obs.N: Right panel: for $N$ = 1, 2, 3, … the levels multiply and fill the shaded bands ($N \to \infty$)
ch41.b.obs.b: Smaller spacing (closer atoms): wider bands and a smaller gap
ch41.b.obs.upper: The upper band is wider than the lower one: higher-energy states tunnel through the barriers more easily
ch41.b.assume.model: Each atom is a square well 0.5 nm wide and 5 eV deep; electron mass; solved numerically by finite differences
ch41.b.assume.kp: Shaded bands: allowed energies of an infinitely repeated well (Kronig-Penney model)
ch41.f.d.mat: A metal, or a semiconductor or insulator with a given band gap
ch41.f.d.scale: Horizontal axis of the occupation probability $f(E)$; a log scale shows very small values
ch41.f.goal.class: How the bands are filled separates metals, semiconductors and insulators
ch41.f.goal.T: Raising the temperature spreads the Fermi-Dirac distribution, lifting valence electrons into the conduction band and leaving holes
ch41.f.obs.metal: Metal: the Fermi level $E_\text{F}$ lies inside a band with empty states just above, so it conducts. Temperature changes only a range $kT$ around $E_\text{F}$
ch41.f.obs.semi: Semiconductor: at 0 K the valence band is full and the conduction band empty, like an insulator. Heating creates electron-hole pairs
ch41.f.obs.ins: Insulator (diamond): the gap is so large that $f(E_c) \approx 10^{-23}$ even at 600 K; practically no conduction electrons
ch41.f.obs.log: Log axis: occupation at the bottom of the conduction band (dot) $\approx e^{-E_\text{g}/2kT}$, Ge > Si ≫ diamond
ch41.f.assume.dots: The number of electron and hole dots grows with the logarithm of $n_i$ (exaggerated); the true ratio is in the $n$ readout and the $f(E)$ graph
ch41.f.assume.param: Effective densities of states $N_c, N_v \propto T^{3/2}$; band gaps fixed, independent of temperature; diamond assumed $N_c = N_v = 10^{19}\ \text{cm}^{-3}$
ch41.f.assume.metal: The metal's bands are schematic; $n$ is the conduction-electron density of sodium
ch41.c.d.fill: Fraction of the band's states occupied by electrons
ch41.c.d.field: Strength of a field pointing right; electrons are pushed the other way
ch41.c.goal.shift: The field changes every electron's wave number $k$ at the same rate; scattering stops the shift at a steady value
ch41.c.goal.full: Only a partly filled band carries current. A full band shifted is the same distribution, so its current is 0
ch41.c.obs.half: Half: the occupied states lean to one side of $k$, so $+v$ and $-v$ no longer cancel: $J > 0$, steady after about $\tau$ = 10 fs
ch41.c.obs.full: Full: electrons pushed past the zone edge ($\pm\pi/a$) come back on the other side, the distribution is unchanged, $J = 0$
ch41.c.obs.nearly: Nearly full: a small current, set by the two empty states (holes)
ch41.c.obs.off: Turn the field off while running: scattering restores the distribution and the current decays exponentially
ch41.c.obs.v: Electron velocity $v = (1/\hbar)\,dE/dk$ is the slope of the curve, zero at the bottom and top of the band
ch41.c.assume.band: One-dimensional band $E(k) = -2t\cos ka$ ($t$ = 1 eV), 32 $k$ states, scattering time $\tau$ = 10 fs
ch41.c.assume.shift: The shift is greatly exaggerated (in a real metal it is a tiny fraction of the zone); scattering is modelled as relaxation of the whole distribution
ch41.d.d.type: Pure silicon, or silicon with donor (n-type) or acceptor (p-type) impurities
ch41.d.d.conc: Number density of donor or acceptor atoms
ch41.d.goal.dope: Donors add levels just below the conduction band, acceptors just above the valence band; they ionise easily at room temperature and supply majority carriers
ch41.d.goal.T: Three regimes of carrier density: freeze-out (cold), extrinsic ($n \approx N_D$), intrinsic (hot, $n \approx n_i$)
ch41.d.obs.n: n-type at 300 K: almost all donors are ionised (⊕), $n \approx N_D$, and $E_\text{F}$ moves up toward the conduction band
ch41.d.obs.p: p-type: acceptors capture valence electrons (⊖) and leave holes; $E_\text{F}$ moves down toward the valence band
ch41.d.obs.freeze: Below about 100 K electrons fall back onto the donors and $n$ drops
ch41.d.obs.intr: Above about 700 K thermal generation across the gap takes over and $n$ follows $n_i$; pure silicon has $n_i \approx 10^{10}\ \text{cm}^{-3}$ at room temperature
ch41.d.obs.law: $np = n_i^2$: more majority carriers means fewer minority carriers
ch41.d.assume.si: Silicon: $E_\text{g}$ = 1.12 eV (fixed, independent of temperature); donor and acceptor ionisation energies 0.045 eV
ch41.d.assume.dots: Eight sites in the picture stand for the dopant density; carrier dots are drawn at the same ratio, capped at 16
